title: Self-defeating Forethought

full_text:
In the city of Kalyanpur lived a miserable, penurious hunter named Bhairava. Though skilled with the bow and successful in his trade, he was so consumed by avarice that he begrudged himself even a handful of parched gram, wearing ragged homespun and hoarding every copper penny he received.

One morning, Bhairava took his heavy composite horn-bow and sharp iron-tipped arrows, setting out into the deep jungle to hunt. He stalked a magnificent, fat spotted deer through the brushwood and brought it down with a clean shot through the heart. Shouldering the heavy carcass, he prepared to turn homeward, overjoyed by his good fortune.

Suddenly, a ferocious, tusked wild boar crossed his path, grunting fiercely. Greed conquered prudence; unwilling to leave the boar behind, the hunter nocked another arrow and shot the beast in the throat. Struck with a mortal wound, the enraged boar charged forward with blinding speed, gored the hunter through his stomach with his razor-sharp tusks, and collapsed dead across the hunter's feet.

At that same moment, a venomous viper disturbed by the struggle struck the boar's snout, dying of the boar's thrashing.

Thus, within a single circle of blood lay four dead bodies: the deer, the wild boar, the hunter, and the serpent!

Presently, a famished, miserly jackal named Dirghamukha wandered into the clearing. Seeing four fat carcasses lying ready for the taking, his little eyes gleamed with ecstasy: 'O divine Fortune! What an inexhaustible mountain of wealth! Here is food to sustain me for three full months!'

Yet his innate, obsessive miserliness asserted itself: 'A prudent beast does not gorge his belly in reckless haste. He eats slowly, saving the best for tomorrow. First, I will eat this thin, tough bowstring made of dried gut; it will satisfy my morning hunger, and I can preserve the succulent meat of the deer, boar, and hunter for future weeks!'

The foolish jackal walked up to the heavy horn-bow lying bent on the turf. He seized the taut, stretched bowstring between his teeth and gnawed on the gut.

The moment his sharp fangs severed the strained cord, the powerful horn-bow uncoiled with the force of an iron catapult. The heavy, sharp-tipped horn end snapped upward like lightning, struck the jackal squarely in the forehead, pierced his brain, and killed him on the spot!

Thus the hoarder died before tasting a single morsel of the vast feast he had hoarded.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"The hoarder starves his living soul to pile his treasures high,
Denying food and charity beneath the open sky;
Yet sudden fate uncoils its spring before his feast is fed,
And leaves the miser in the dust among his treasures dead."
moral: Extreme stinginess that hoards without enjoyment or charity leads to sudden and ironic loss.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "Self-defeating Forethought"?
options: Loyal friendship and mutual trust overcome the greatest hardships.
Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
quiz.hint: Remember the moral lesson of this traditional story.

quiz.question: How do the characters overcome their challenge?
options: Through patience, calm reflection, and wisdom
By shouting loudly and blaming others
By running away from every problem
quiz.hint: Consider the virtues praised in world folklore.

quiz.question: What memorable conclusion does this story teach young readers?
options: Honesty, kindness, and clear thinking lead to peace
quiz.hint: Reflect upon the resolution of the story.

author: Pandit Vishnu Sharma (~200 BCE – 300 CE)
